title: Implement Player comparison
lead: Keep playback alive for seeking and delivery observations, and use explicitly defined browser timings.

blocks.text: Keep one playback session for each player

Within each measured session, the loaded player and video element stay available for its seek and delivery observations; a source reload is not counted as seek latency. After measurements finish, the UI keeps or recreates a successfully measured player for preview without changing the measurement records. If no player succeeds, playback controls stay disabled. Measurement runs are sequential. Parallel visual previews remain separate from numerical comparison.

rows: The common 360p HLS uses a composition of public Web X packages. Custom URLs, the adaptive HLS ladder and DASH use their format-specific prebuilt bundles. The native Player and Source APIs are used throughout. DASH support in 10.3.1 is partial, so a manifest that plays in Shaka may still be incompatible. Observers are registered before loading or playback, and the player is disposed when its session ends.
Use modular MSE playback for the selected HLS/DASH format, attach the shared video element, await load, then request play. Keep Ready, load completion and Playing as separate observations.
Attach Hls to the video element and load the HLS source. DASH is explicitly unsupported. Destroy the instance when its session ends.
Use a build that supports the selected HLS or DASH format. Observe load and play separately and await destruction during cleanup.

blocks.text: Custom source URLs remain in the current playback session. Results use safe identifiers rather than storing or exporting the URL. Cancellation and session cleanup remove app-owned SDK/video listeners and frame callbacks.
Name each interval and observation

Use the same parent performance clock for each player’s accepted Measure trial, SDK import, initialization, loading, play requests and browser callbacks. The primary startup interval begins before creating the fresh playback document and ends at the first moving-frame observation. Initialization and load can overlap; adding their durations does not reconstruct startup time.

The accepted measurement is per player, not the original physical button-click time. Network mode prepares its Service Worker before accepting that measurement, so worker preparation is excluded while SDK import, player creation and loading remain included.

The main moving-frame observation uses requestVideoFrameCallback and checks that media time advances. It records when the callback is observed, not the physical display time. Native playing, SDK Ready, the load promise and loadeddata are separate observations; none is substituted for a missing frame callback.

A successful startup needs the adapter’s play operation, native playing and actual playback progress, with moving frames checked when callbacks are supported. Browser API limitations can leave a frame latency unavailable even when playback works. Failure, cancellation and unsupported operations remain explicit outcomes.
Observe the target and its moving frame

Choose a target from the valid seekable range and record whether it is buffered at the request. Start the interval when requesting the seek. Completion requires the native seeking event, a frame within 0.25 seconds of the target and subsequent media-time advancement greater than 0.01 seconds. The observation has a 10-second budget. The seeked event or a frame from the old position cannot complete it.

Without frame callbacks, retain an unsupported or unavailable reason instead of creating a zero-valued seek result. Read in-buffer and out-of-buffer seeks separately: fetching new media is a different condition from presenting data already buffered.
Separate delivery control from observations

Network mode retains normal playback through the configured rate phases and observes quality and stalls. It does not perform the measured seek used in Startup and seek; that latency remains unmeasured rather than zero.

Delivery control is limited to the bundled Big Buck Bunny fixture. Custom HLS/DASH URLs can be used for startup and seeking; their Network change control is disabled because full media coverage cannot be established.

The fixture opts into a narrowly scoped Service Worker and paces decoded media response bodies under one shared byte-per-second budget. Original CORS and credential rules remain. Opaque, redirected or unclassified responses are skipped or unsupported; SDK downloads and license requests are excluded. This is response-body delivery control, not physical bandwidth, round-trip latency or cache emulation.

Control status reports the requested rate, shaped responses, delivered bytes and skipped responses without URLs. Check these observations before claiming that an engine’s media was shaped: worker-originated SDK requests may not belong to the opted-in client. A configured cap alone is not measured throughput.

Validate each rate phase with a positive delivered-byte delta during that phase. Earlier bytes in a cumulative counter cannot qualify a later phase. If no bytes are delivered while a phase is active, retain the missing or unsupported outcome rather than reporting successful control.

Plot only observed quality changes, delivery samples and stalls. Keep an SDK’s quality or bandwidth estimate separate from the configured cap. Do not invent an adaptive-quality transition for a single-rendition source, or fill a missing provider value with a synthetic sample.
Keep the advanced benchmark separate

The retained benchmark still creates a fresh document and video element for each isolated startup trial. Its fixed-rendition HLS, import-mode controls, default/startup profiles, candidate screening and independent confirmation belong to that experiment. They do not turn a parallel preview or retained seek session into an isolated startup trial.

That benchmark keeps en-labelled audio, muted playback, normal rate and start position zero. Its startup retention candidate is 12 seconds forward and 6 seconds behind, not a total-memory limit. Screening varies hls.js enableWorker true/false and Shaka segmentPrefetchLimit 0/1/2; Web X keeps loadControl=2 (Data). Each isolated trial has the existing 30-second deadline. SDK preloading describes import timing, not a warm HTTP cache.

Repository source links below are the retained benchmark snapshot. They explain that implementation and its export/ranking rules; they are not source evidence for the new retained-playback and delivery-control paths. The 2026-11-01 report remains historical.
Read unavailable values without guessing

items: Provider events keep their own meanings. Web X Source ready, hls.js manifest parsing and Shaka loaded are not interchangeable moving-frame timestamps.
A quality getter or bandwidth estimate may be unavailable for a player. Unknown does not mean zero bandwidth or poor playback.

Browser caching, request concurrency, decoding and tab activity affect the observations. Sequential runs reduce contention between players; they do not establish identical device or network conditions.

blocks.text: Implementation FAQ
Why can a custom DASH manifest fail in Web X?

Player Web X 10.3.1 cannot handle some MPDs using $RepresentationID$ or $Number%05d$ templates. Use a compatible MPD. The app passes the custom URL unchanged: it does not rewrite the manifest, patch the SDK or convert a failure into a zero-millisecond success. Selecting DASH does not promise compatibility with every MPD.
Does one successful run establish smooth playback?

No. Read the startup, seek and delivery observations as different checks. A successful short run does not establish long-session stability or a generally fastest SDK. No prerecorded result is displayed as a measurement of the current run.
Is the moving-frame graph Analytics VST?

No. This comparison uses browser observations with explicit origins. Bitmovin Analytics VIDEO_STARTUPTIME uses Play → TimeChanged; STARTUPTIME also includes PLAYER_STARTUPTIME. Playing and moving-frame observations are not a replacement for those collector-defined values. This comparison does not enable a collector or synthesize Dashboard values.
